The located literature does not establish that content-dependent dilation gates outperform parameter-matched capacity, fixed multiscale branches, and shorter windows simultaneously. Closest evidence: SkipRec adapts NextItNet’s residual-block execution per user. Its learned policy beats random skipping; versions trained from scratch show less overfitting, but converge more slowly than the full backbone. This supports adaptive computation, not specifically stale-context rejection or adaptive dilation. Reported inference savings should not be interpreted as training savings. [SkipRec, AAAI 2021](https://cdn.aaai.org/ojs/16518/16518-13-20012-1-2-20210518.pdf)

Extra parameters are an inadequate explanation by themselves: CpRec’s controlled adjacent-block sharing ablation halves NextItNet’s middle-layer parameters while improving ML20 HR@5 from 0.1755 to 0.1762. Its complete compression configuration achieves HR@5 0.1765, reduces total parameters from 62M to 15M, and training to convergence from 104 to 64 minutes. These ordinary recommendation experiments require no pretrained models; however, their compression and softmax changes do not isolate context selection. [CpRec, ablations and training costs](https://arxiv.org/html/2004.13139)

Recommended decisive experiment: compare ordinary NextItNet, a parameter-matched ungated control, identical dilation branches with uniform weights, learned input-independent weights, content-dependent gates, and shorter history windows. Train each configuration from scratch with fixed splits, sampling, seeds, and optimization budget. Diagnose stale-context sensitivity by removing or perturbing only old prefixes while preserving recent suffixes; measure validation HR@10 changes by history length and timestamp gap. Gate shuffling across users provides an additional test of content dependence. Report parameters, GPU-seconds, throughput, and accuracy at equal elapsed budgets. These are proposed controls, not published findings; prioritize a small gate trial only if it beats static branches and truncation within the training budget.
